Design choices Hand assembly: 0603/0805 passives, SOIC-8, LQFP-48. No BGA, no fine-pitch QFN. Cost: the N8 module (no PSRAM) and a single-chip PoE module keep the BOM small. IN and OUT per port: two terminals in parallel on one transceiver for daisy chaining. Expansion: header J5 for a third port or other add-ons. More detail: docs/12-pcb-design-notes.md .

Power tree flowchart LR USB[USB-C VBUS] --> F1[PTC F1 1.1 A] --> D3[D3 SS14] --> V5 POE[PoE via RJ45] --> PS1[DP9700-5V] --> X[5V_EXT] J6[J6 header] --> X X --> D4[D4 SS14] --> V5[+5V rail] V5 --> U5[AMS1117-3.3] --> V33[+3V3] V5 --> D5[D5 SS14] --> LV[LED_VDD to WS2812B] Diode-OR: USB (via D3) and 5V_EXT (via D4) feed +5V , so they never back-feed each other. +5V is not a clean 5.0 V: it is the source minus one SS14 drop, about 4.5-4.7 V loaded. This is also what J5 pin 2 provides. 3.3 V: AMS1117-3.3 with 10 µF in and 22 µF out. Bulk caps: C5 and C50, 220 µF 6.3 V (thin margin, see Roadmap ). Caution The PoE module output and the J6 header are the same net ( 5V_EXT ) with no diode between them. Use only one of them at a time. Never put an external supply on J6 while PoE is powering the board. Current budget (estimates, verify on the bench) Load Typical Peak ESP32-S3 (Wi-Fi TX) 100-150 mA @ 3.3 V 350-400 mA W5500 ~130 mA @ 3.3 V ~150 mA 2 × SN65HVD72 + bias < 20 mA ~25 mA each driving, +5.5 mA bias WS2812B 1-10 mA 60 mA white The 3.3 V rail can reach roughly 500-600 mA at peaks, or 0.6-0.8 A on the 5 V side. That is more than a default 500 mA USB port . On USB alone expect brownouts with Wi-Fi and Ethernet both busy. Use PoE or an external 5 V supply for real use. Grounding and protection One GND plane joins USB, DMX and logic. Nothing isolates DMX from USB, so a laptop on USB plus a long DMX run at a different earth can create a ground loop. Use an isolated USB hub, or see isolated DMX in the Roadmap . The PoE module is isolated (1.5 kV per its datasheet). The RJ45 shield ( CHASSIS ) ties to GND through 10 nF and 1 MΩ in parallel. USB has a USBLC6-2SC6; each DMX port has an SM712 TVS. There is no extra surge protection on the 5 V inputs beyond the USB PTC.

Two identical ports. Each uses one SN65HVD72DR (3.3 V, half-duplex, 250 kbps) with its fail-safe receiver for open, shorted and idle buses, which keeps the RX line quiet during RDM listen windows. Part DMX1 DMX2 Transceiver U3 U4 TVS (SM712) D1 D2 Bias resistors 240 Ω R31, R32 R41, R42 Bias switch (2N7002) Q1 Q2 Termination 120 Ω R34 R44 Termination jumper J2T J3T IN / OUT terminals J2 / J2O J3 / J3O Port LED D30 D40 MCU pins UART1 TX17 RX16 DIR39 UART2 TX15 RX18 DIR40 DIR drives /RE and DE together. High = transmit, low = receive. A 10 kΩ pull-down keeps the port receiving while the MCU is in reset. Bias: BIAS1/BIAS2 (GPIO1/2) high turns on a 240 Ω pull-up on A and a 240 Ω pull-down on B. Off by default. Termination: a shunt on J2T/J3T puts 120 Ω across A and B. Only on the last device of a line. Protection: SM712 per port (-7 V to +12 V). No isolation, no series fuse. Note Bias values were chosen by the designer, not taken from the E1.20 text. Expect about 0.6 V idle differential into a terminated line and about 5.5 mA bias current. Board terminal XLR pin Signal GND 1 Shield / common B 2 Data − (as labelled) A 3 Data + (as labelled) 5-pin XLR pins 4 and 5 are not connected. Warning A/B polarity is not verified on hardware. RS-485 vendors disagree on which line is "A". Test with a known-good fixture or a DMX tester; if the fixture does not respond, swap the two wires. IN and OUT IN and OUT on a port are two terminals on the same bus (A to A, B to B, GND to GND). They are not a repeater. A port is a source or a sink for the whole port, and a daisy chain continues from the OUT terminal. flowchart LR N[Node port] --- F1[Fixture 1] --- F2[Fixture 2] --- F3[Fixture 3 + 120 Ω terminator] Good practice Use DMX or RS-485 cable (120 Ω twisted pair), not microphone cable, for long runs. Terminate only the last device. On the node, fit the J2T/J3T shunt only if the node is last. Keep stubs short; daisy chain rather than T-splitting. Enable bias only if no other device on the line provides it. Watch for ground loops between USB and a lighting rig on a different earth ( Power ).

Hot air or a hotplate makes the W5500, ESP32 module and USB-C connector much easier. Order of work Hardest first - U2 W5500 (LQFP-48, 0.5 mm): tack two corners, flux, drag-solder, clean bridges with braid. - J4 USB-C: signal pins first, then shield posts. - U1 ESP32-S3: castellated pads and the centre ground pad. Antenna end hangs at the board edge with nothing under it. SOIC / SOT: U3, U4, U5 (tab to the large pad), U6, Q1, Q2, D1, D2. Passives: 0603 first, then 0805 (C1, C6, C7, C14, C17, C18). Crystal Y1 has no polarity. Polarised parts - D3, D4, D5 (SS14): cathode band toward the +5V side (D5 toward LED_VDD ). - D30, D40 LEDs: cathode to GND. - LED1 WS2812B: pin 1 marked on the board. - C5, C50: + mark toward the 5 V rail. Through-hole: headers, screw terminals (wire entry toward the edge), J1 RJ45, and PS1 last because it covers most of the board. Shunts on J2T/J3T only if the node is the last device on a DMX line. Is it tested? No. rev1 has not been manufactured, and the firmware changes are unbuilt. Why N8 instead of N16R8? The firmware is about 1.1 MB and does not need PSRAM, so the cheaper module is enough. Why SN65HVD72? It is a 250 kbps part with receiver fail-safe for open, short and idle buses, which suits DMX and RDM. The SP3485 is only fail-safe for open inputs and has weaker ESD. Can I use a different RS-485 chip? Yes if it uses the standard SOIC-8 pinout, states open/short/idle fail-safe and has adequate ESD. Does it do RDM? Hardware is bidirectional and the firmware has an RDM stack; neither has been tested on this board. Can I skip PoE? Yes. Leave PS1 and C50 unpopulated and use USB or J6. Can I add a third port? J5 provides UART0, DIR3, BIAS3, LED3 and spare GPIOs. UART0 is shared with the debug header, so use USB as console. Why 100 × 100 mm? JLCPCB's cheapest price tier has historically stopped there. Can I sell it? The licence allows it (CERN-OHL-P-2.0, permissive). The name "Ghostlight Node" is not trademark-cleared. Why does the firmware say ESP-NODE-2RDM? That is the original firmware project name; the board is still reported under it.

The Ghostlight Node receives lighting data over the network (Art-Net or sACN over Ethernet, optionally Wi-Fi) and outputs it as DMX512 on two physical ports. Both ports use half-duplex RS-485 with direction control, so the hardware supports RDM (discovery and responder) as well as plain DMX output or input. Whether a given feature works is decided by the firmware. PoE module and J6 share one net : the DP9700 output and the J6 header are connected directly together on 5V_EXT , with no diode between them. Use only one of them at a time. Do not put an external 5 V supply on J6 while a PoE module is powered, and do not power J6 from a different regulated supply than the PoE module output, or the two supplies will fight each other. Rail voltage : +5V is the source voltage minus one SS14 drop, so roughly 4.5-4.7 V when loaded. This is the voltage on J5 pin 2 ("5V") and on the WS2812 supply path. It is not a regulated 5.0 V. 3.3 V : AMS1117-3.3 (U5) with 10 uF in (C6) and 22 uF out (C7). The LDO dropout (about 1.1 V at 1 A) is covered by the 4.5 V rail. R2 (330 ohm) is in series with the data line. Current budget (estimates, verify on the bench) Load Typical Peak ESP32-S3 (Wi-Fi TX peaks) ~100-150 mA at 3.3 V up to ~350-400 mA W5500 ~130 mA at 3.3 V ~150 mA 2 x SN65HVD72 + bias networks < 20 mA ~25 mA each when driving, plus ~5.5 mA bias when enabled WS2812B ~1-10 mA (one LED at low brightness) 60 mA at full white The 3.3 V rail can reach roughly 500-600 mA at the peaks, which is about 0.6-0.8 A on the 5 V side once the LDO's pass-through is counted. That is above the 500 mA a default USB port may supply . On USB alone, expect brownouts if Wi-Fi and Ethernet are both active at full load; use PoE or an external supply for real use. AMS1117 power dissipation is (V_in - 3.3 V) x I, about 0.5-0.7 W at 0.5 A with a 4.6 V input, which the SOT-223 tab and the copper pour handle but will run warm. Isolation and grounding A single GND plane connects USB, the DMX terminals, and the logic. The PoE module is isolated (1.5 kV per the module datasheet), so the Ethernet side and shield ( CHASSIS ) are separate from GND on the PoE side. The RJ45 shield ( CHASSIS ) is tied to GND through C23 (10 nF) and R12 (1 M) in parallel. Because nothing isolates the DMX ports from USB, plugging in a laptop while a long DMX run is connected to a different earth can cause ground loops. Use an isolated USB hub or an isolated RS-485 version on rev2 if this matters. ESD and surge USB: USBLC6-2SC6 on D+ / D- (VBUS pin also tied). DMX: one SM712 asymmetric TVS (A, B, GND) per port. This clamps to -7 V / +12 V, matching RS-485 common-mode limits. No extra surge protection on the 5 V inputs beyond the PTC on USB.

Tools: temperature-controlled iron with a fine tip, flux, fine solder (0.5 mm), tweezers, desoldering braid, magnification, multimeter. Hot air or a hotplate makes the W5500, the ESP32 module and the USB-C connector much easier. Look at the silkscreen photo in the README for reference designators and orientation. Order Smallest and most difficult first - U2 (W5500, LQFP-48, 0.5 mm pitch). Tack two opposite corners, flux, drag-solder, then clean up bridges with braid. Pin 1 is marked on the silkscreen. - J4 (USB-C, 16 pin with through-hole shield tabs). Solder the signal pins first, then the shield posts. - U1 (ESP32-S3 module): solder the castellated pads and the central thermal pad (ground). The antenna end must hang at the board edge with nothing under it. SOIC / SOT : U3, U4 (SN65HVD72, pin 1 dot toward the silkscreen 1 marker), U5 (AMS1117, tab to the large pad), U6 (USBLC6), Q1, Q2, D1, D2 (SM712 is a 3-pin SOT-23). Passives : 0603 resistors and capacitors; 0805 capacitors (C1, C6, C14, C18, C7, C17). Take care with the crystal Y1 (3225, 4 pads; there is no polarity but keep the part flat). Polarised parts - Schottky diodes D3, D4, D5 (SS14, SMA): the cathode band goes to the +5V side for D3 and D4 (the rail), and to the LED supply ( LED_VDD ) side for D5. Check against the silkscreen. - LEDs D30, D40: cathode to GND . Check the green marker on the part. - WS2812B (LED1): pin 1 marked with "1" on the board. - Electrolytics C5, C50: + mark on the board marks the positive terminal, toward the +5V rail / 5V_EXT . - PTC F1 and ferrite L1 have no polarity. Through-hole : pin headers J5, J6, J7, J2T, J3T (snap from the 1x40 strip), screw terminals J2, J2O, J3, J3O (wire entry toward the board edge), J1 RJ45, then PS1 (PoE module) last because it sits over most of the board. Fit shunts on J2T / J3T only if the board is the last device on a DMX line. After soldering Visual check under magnification: bridges on the W5500, USB-C, ESP32 and SOIC pins, correct orientation of diodes, LEDs, and electrolytics. Continuity with the board unpowered: +3V3 to GND and +5V to GND must not be a short (expect resistance in the hundreds of ohms to kilohms depending on the multimeter, not near zero). Clean flux off with isopropyl alcohol. Go to docs/10 .

Do these in order. Stop and investigate at the first failure. Use a bench power supply with current limiting if you have one. Never connect PoE first. 0. Before power Check Expected Resistance +5V to GND not a short Resistance +3V3 to GND not a short USB-C CC1 / CC2 to GND about 5.1 k each (R3, R4) Diode orientation (D3, D4, D5) cathode toward the +5V side 1. USB power only Plug in USB-C (preferably through a powered hub or a bench supply set to 5 V, current limit about 300 mA first). Measure Expected +5V rail about 4.5-4.7 V (VBUS minus the SS14 and PTC drop) +3V3 rail 3.3 V +/- 5 % Supply current, nothing flashed well under 100 mA Component temperatures nothing too hot to touch in the first minute (U5 may be warm) 2. Flash and console Hold BOOT, tap RESET, release BOOT. Confirm the USB device appears, flash the firmware, and read the console (USB or J7 at 3.3 V logic). Confirm the ESP32 boots and the status LED responds. 3. Ethernet Connect a normal (non-PoE) switch or router with a patch cable. The jack's link and activity LEDs should light and the firmware should report a link and obtain an IP. If the W5500 is not detected: probe the 25 MHz crystal, check 3V3 on the W5500 AVDD pins and the SPI lines (CS, SCK, MOSI, MISO), the RST and INT pull-ups, then compare the analog network to the WIZnet reference ( docs/11 ). Ping the node and send Art-Net or sACN. 4. DMX Connect a scope or logic analyser to A and B (use differential probing or probe A and B separately against GND). Send a DMX frame. Confirm 250 kbaud, break and mark-after-break timing, and that the receive pin is quiet when DIR is low and the bus is idle. Check the A / B polarity against a known-good fixture or DMX tester and fix the labelling or wiring if needed. With BIAS on, measure the idle differential on the line (should be above 200 mV into a terminated line) and confirm the receiver stays quiet (no phantom RDM responses). Verify each port's termination jumper by measuring about 120 ohm across A and B with it fitted and the bus idle. Check both ports, and both IN and OUT terminals, independently. 5. PoE (last) Check the PoE module orientation and the 5V_EXT voltage with a lab PoE source or an 802.3af injector before connecting a load. With USB disconnected, power through an 802.3af switch port. Expect the module output near 5 V and the board to boot. Verify 5V_EXT, +5V and +3V3 under load (Wi-Fi + Ethernet + both DMX ports active). Connect USB at the same time as PoE: nothing should back-feed (diode-OR), and current should not flow from one source into the other. Record results Please open an issue with the results (scope screenshots of A/B, voltages, any wiring changes) so rev2 can be corrected.

None of these firmware changes have been applied or tested ; they were written from reading the firmware's board.h , sdkconfig.defaults , partitions.csv and network_manager.c . Status: sections 1, 2 and the port-LED part of 3 are already applied in firmware/ . The build and the partition table are untested (no ESP-IDF was available); the 8 MB table was checked only for overlaps, 64 KB app alignment and total size (ends at 0x770000). Regenerate sdkconfig before building. 1. Required: switch from N16R8 to the N8 module The firmware currently assumes 16 MB flash and 8 MB octal PSRAM. The N8 module has 8 MB quad flash and no PSRAM . In sdkconfig.defaults : # replace CONFIG_ESPTOOLPY_FLASHSIZE_16MB=y # with CONFIG_ESPTOOLPY_FLASHSIZE_8MB=y # remove these (no PSRAM on the N8: with SPIRAM_BOOT_INIT enabled the boot fails) CONFIG_SPIRAM=y CONFIG_SPIRAM_MODE_OCT=y CONFIG_SPIRAM_SPEED_80M=y CONFIG_SPIRAM_BOOT_INIT=y CONFIG_SPIRAM_MALLOC_RESERVE_INTERNAL=32768 Delete sdkconfig (or run idf.py fullclean and regenerate) after editing the defaults, because the existing generated sdkconfig keeps the old values. CONFIG_ESPTOOLPY_FLASHMODE_DIO and 80 MHz flash can stay. The firmware allocates its diagnostic log ring from PSRAM with a fallback to internal RAM ( components/diag/diag.c ), so no code change is required for that, but check heap use with the larger buffers (Art-Net / sACN receive buffers, web UI) once PSRAM is gone. 2. The board and schematic were produced by Python scripts, kept in tools/generator/ . They are included for reference and reproducibility of the netlist and placement ; the committed board and gerbers are the source of truth for manufacturing. The routed result is not reproducible bit-for-bit (the autorouter is non-deterministic). The scripts contain absolute paths from the machine where they ran ( /home/claude/pcb ) and expect KiCad 7's Python ( pcbnew ), kiutils , Java + Freerouting 1.9.0 and xvfb-run . You will need to edit the paths before running anything. Pipeline Step Script What it does 1 design.py single source of truth: parts, values, footprints and nets 2 layout.py placement overrides 3 build_pcb.py creates the .kicad_pcb with footprints, outline, mounting holes and nets 4 route.py / import_ses.py sets the design rules (0.15 mm clearance, 0.2 mm track, 0.5 / 0.3 mm via), removes the pours so GND is routed as copper, exports a Specctra DSN, runs Freerouting, then imports the session (SES) back 5 finish.py post-route clean-up: island removal, GND stitching vias, solid ground pads on the USB-C shield, zone refill 6 widen.py widens the +3V3 , +5V , VBUS , VBUS_F and 5V_EXT tracks (0.5 / 0.35 / 0.25 mm steps, where space allows) 7 drc.py runs KiCad's DRC through pcbnew and prints the violation counts 8 silk.py adds the silkscreen labels, title block and back-side text 9 gen_sch.py generates the net-label schematic and the ESPNODE.kicad_sym symbol library 10 bom.py writes BOM_order.csv and BOM_order_purchase.csv chain.sh runs steps 3-7 (step 8, silk.py , is run separately on the finished board) in order ( MP = Freerouting pass limit); search.sh repeats it with different pass limits until DRC is clean. Overview The DMX Handler component provides a unified interface for controlling 2 independent DMX512/RDM ports on the ESP-NODE-2RDM device. It wraps the esp-dmx library and provides high-level APIs for DMX output, input, and RDM operations. Features Dual Independent Ports : 2 fully independent DMX512/RDM ports Multiple Modes : DMX Output, DMX Input, RDM Master, RDM Responder High Performance : ~44Hz DMX refresh rate Thread-Safe : All APIs protected with mutexes Flexible Configuration : Per-port mode and universe assignment Statistics : Frame counters and error tracking Callback Support : Asynchronous notifications for received data and RDM discovery Hardware Configuration Port 1 TX Pin : GPIO 17 RX Pin : GPIO 16 Direction Pin : GPIO 21 UART : UART_NUM_1 Port 2 TX Pin : GPIO 19 RX Pin : GPIO 18 Direction Pin : GPIO 20 UART : UART_NUM_2 RS485 Transceiver Each port requires an RS485 transceiver (e.g., MAX485, MAX3485) with: - TX connected to MCU TX pin - RX connected to MCU RX pin - DE/RE connected to MCU Direction pin Port Modes DMX_MODE_OUTPUT (0) Standard DMX512 output mode: - Continuously sends 512 channels at ~44Hz - No RDM support - Lowest latency DMX_MODE_INPUT (1) DMX512 input/monitoring mode: - Receives DMX frames from upstream controller - Triggers callback on frame reception - Can read last received frame DMX_MODE_RDM_MASTER (2) DMX output with RDM master capability: - Sends DMX frames at ~44Hz - Can perform RDM discovery - Can GET/SET RDM parameters - Controls RDM responder devices DMX_MODE_RDM_RESPONDER (3) RDM responder mode: - Responds to RDM discovery - Responds to RDM GET/SET commands - Allows configuration via RDM controllers DMX_MODE_DISABLED (4) Port disabled: - No DMX transmission or reception - Driver uninstalled - Lowest power consumption API Reference Initialization esp_err_t dmx_handler_init(void) Initialize the DMX handler module. Must be called before any other functions. Returns: - ESP_OK on success - ESP_ERR_NO_MEM if memory allocation failed - ESP_ERR_INVALID_STATE if already initialized Example: ESP_ERROR_CHECK(dmx_handler_init()); esp_err_t dmx_handler_deinit(void) Deinitialize the module and free resources. Port Configuration esp_err_t dmx_handler_configure_port(uint8_t port, const port_config_t *config) Configure a port with mode and universe settings. Parameters: - port : Port number (1 or 2) - config : Port configuration from config_manager Returns: - ESP_OK on success - ESP_ERR_INVALID_ARG if parameters invalid - ESP_FAIL if configuration failed Example: config_t *config = config_get(); ESP_ERROR_CHECK(dmx_handler_configure_port(DMX_PORT_1, &config->port1)); esp_err_t dmx_handler_start_port(uint8_t port) Start a configured port. Example: ESP_ERROR_CHECK(dmx_handler_start_port(DMX_PORT_1)); esp_err_t dmx_handler_stop_port(uint8_t port) Stop a running port. DMX Output esp_err_t dmx_handler_send_dmx(uint8_t port, const uint8_t *data) Send a complete DMX frame (512 channels). ESPHome external component for Wi-Fi HaLow (IEEE 802.11ah) using the Morse Micro MM6108 . It replaces wifi: with halow: : configure the SSID, password and region in YAML, and the device joins a HaLow access point with full IP networking, so the Home Assistant API, OTA updates, mDNS and MQTT all work over sub-1 GHz radio with up to ~1 km range. This is a fork of sweitzja/esphome-halow . It makes the component build and run on ESPHome 2026.x (the native ESP-IDF toolchain used by the Home Assistant ESPHome Builder) and fixes bugs found in review, including Home Assistant connections being dropped on 2026.x. Every change is listed with its reasoning in PATCHES.md . The state before the review fixes is kept on the pre-improvements branch. Why HaLow over LoRa? HaLow uses standard IP networking: TCP, UDP, DHCP, mDNS, MQTT and the ESPHome API all work natively, with no protocol translation, gateway bridges or TTN accounts. A HaLow device is just another IP device on your network that Home Assistant sees directly, OTA updates work over the same link, and bidirectional control is fast (~7 ms). LoRa still wins on raw range (10-15 km vs ~1 km) and power for simple one-way sensors; for anything that needs reliable two-way communication, HaLow is much cleaner. Integration points 1. network::is_connected() / get_ip_addresses() (critical) What: ESPHome's API server disconnects every client when network::is_connected() is false, then reboots after reboot_timeout . Project Overview OpenCarKey is a DIY keyless entry system with two components: - Firmware/LockController/ — ESP32 firmware (C++, PlatformIO) - MobileApp/ — Flutter Android/iOS app Build & Run Commands Mobile App cd MobileApp flutter pub get flutter run # run on connected device flutter build apk --release # release APK dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs # regenerate freezed files Firmware Open Firmware/LockController/ in PlatformIO. Use PlatformIO's Upload button or: cd Firmware/LockController pio run --target upload pio device monitor --baud 115200 # serial monitor Architecture BLE Protocol (V4) All app→ESP32 messages: 32-byte HMAC-SHA256 + 1-byte command + optional [length byte + data] All ESP32→app messages: 1-byte response + optional [length byte + data] HMAC covers (counter_le4 || command_byte) ; key = SHA-256 of the password. Per-device rolling counter stored in NVS (ESP32) and SharedPreferences (app). Acceptance window is counter .. counter+2 (one-sided). To reset: hold BOOT button on ESP32 for 10 seconds, or use the in-app resync flow. NVS wear protection : the ESP32 keeps counters in a RAM dirty-cache ( _dirtyCounters ) written through to NVS on a 1.5 s debounce during the session ( writeCounter / flushAllCounters ) and on disconnect. The debounce is essential on a car: the ESP32 resets without a clean disconnect all the time (brownout on engine crank, watchdog, power glitch) — flushing only on disconnect rolled the counter backward on every such reset and desynced every phone. readCounter checks the dirty cache before NVS (covers quick reconnects). Both the debounced flush and the disconnect flush run on the BLE task, so there's no cross-core race on _dirtyCounters . Auto-resync : on INVALID_HMAC the app silently sends RESYNC_COUNTER (HMAC proves password knowledge, payload = app's current counter) and starts a 4 s resyncTimer on BackgroundVehicle . COUNTER_RESYNCED cancels the timer (silent success → re-fetch state via GET_DATA ); further INVALID_HMAC s while the timer is live are ignored (collapses the connect-handshake burst into one resync). Only if the timer fires (no confirmation → genuinely wrong password) does the background emit an auth_failed event, which is the only trigger for the reset dialog. Raw INVALID_HMAC must never open the dialog directly — that surfaces a reset prompt for routine, auto-recoverable desyncs. HMAC failures are rate-limited per MAC: 5 failures in 30 s → disconnect + 60 s lockout. All ESP32 responses are broadcast to every connected phone ( pCharacteristic->notify() has no per-connection targeting). Any per-phone filtering must happen app-side. The ESP32 advertises DEVICE_NAME in plain text; the app's scan dialog filters by service UUID 0000ffe0-… (characteristic 0000ffe1-… ), not by name. Commit Message Guidelines For your commit messages please follow Conventional Commits . (If you are using VS Code you can use this extension to help you follow this convention) Structure: - Use the following format for commit messages: type: subject or type(scope): subject Type: A brief type of change (e.g., feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore). Scope (Optional): The section of the codebase that the change affects (e.g., component, module). Subject: A short description of the change (e.g., "add new login feature"). Examples: - feat(auth): add user login - fix(api): handle null values in response - docs: update installation instructions Body (Optional): - Use the body to explain what changes you made and why you made them. Wrap the body at 72 characters per line. Footer (Optional): - Use the footer to reference any related issues or breaking changes. For example: BREAKING CHANGE: refactor authentication middleware Closes #123 Pull Request Guidelines If you modified something in Assets/SmartifyOS keep in mind that anything in there should not be (too) project (car/setup) specific. Title: - Use a clear and descriptive title for the pull request that describes the change being made (also use Conventional Commits here!).
